FRIDAY UPDATE: Jackson County Sheriff’s Department issued the following statement about the incident on Friday morning.

Yesterday an individual identified as 59-year-old, David Ray Wyrick of Eden, NC, used a vehicle loaded with chemical tanks and a firearm to cause damage to a communications tower located behind the Jackson County Emergency Operations Center on Convent Ave. in Pascagoula near the Jackson County Courthouse.

Jackson County Deputies, Criminal Investigators as well as members of the Jackson County Metro Enforcement Team responded to that location and were engaged with gunfire by Wyrick. Those same deputies and officers returned fire and after a brief gunbattle, Wyrick was hit multiple times and died at the scene.

The tanks on the truck were ablaze for a brief period but were quickly secured by Jackson County Fire Personnel.

As a precaution, Jackson County Deputies, with the assistance of many state, local and federal officers, cleared the Jackson County Courthouse, Courthouse Annex and Jackson County General Services Complex of any potential threats and used Explosive Detection K-9s to sweep the area.

No law enforcement officers or citizens were injured in this incident.

We at the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office want to extend our deep gratitude to not only our Deputies but to our law enforcement partners who responded to a rapidly evolving situation, ran towards the gunfire and took action to protect lives and critical infrastructure.

This incident is currently under investigation by Mississippi Bureau of Investigations, with the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The last few weeks have been very challenging for the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office, and we once again wish to acknowledge our dedicated Deputies and the support of our partner agencies at the state, local and federal level as well as the people of Jackson County.

The following is a statement from Special Agent In-Charge Robert Eikhoff F.B.I. Jackson Field Office

“The prompt actions of law enforcement officers prevented a significant disaster. The FBI Jackson Field Office is supporting the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office in this investigation by providing specialized resources as needed. The FBI remains committed to strong collaboration with local and state law enforcement partners across Mississippi.”

ORIGINAL STORY, published Thursday afternoon:

PASCAGOULA – The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation is investigating an officer-involved shooting involving the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office and Gautier Police Department that happened April 16 near Magnolia Street in Pascagoula.

According to MBI, the incident happened at about 12:20 p.m.

Investigators said the subject allegedly drove a vehicle through a fence and parked near a large propane tank. Authorities said the subject then tried to ignite propane tanks in the back of the vehicle in an apparent attempt to cause an explosion.

When law enforcement officers arrived, the subject ran from the scene, leading to a brief pursuit, MBI said.

During the pursuit, an exchange of gunfire occurred between the subject and law enforcement, according to investigators. The subject was fatally injured. No officers or deputies suffered any serious physical injuries.

MBI said the FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are also involved in the investigation.

The bureau said it is continuing to assess the incident and gather evidence. Once the investigation is complete, agents will turn over their findings to the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office.

MBI said the information released so far is preliminary and subject to change. Additional information may be released later.

Moving more and eating better will benefit you, your friends and family, and the entire great state of Mississippi. Participants can choose to compete individually or join a team to turn the experience into a fun and friendly challenge with friends.

Join Extension’s Magnolia Moves Activity Challenge today and let’s get moving together!

STATEWIDE — As we navigate deep political and cultural divisions, International Day of Mastering Conversations That Matter offers a timely reminder: progress often begins with a conversation, and the willingness to truly listen.

Observed each year on April 17, the day highlights the role meaningful, respectful dialogue has played throughout human history, from ancient debating societies in Greece and India to modern discussions that shape public policy, relationships and social change. According to NationalToday.com, the exchange of ideas, debated, refined and shared, has driven everything from scientific advancement to the rise and fall of civilizations.

But in today’s climate, many of those conversations are breaking down. Throw in the phenomenon that is the internet bully, and it’s almost a lost cause. But just ALMOST.

Psychologists say the problem is not actually disagreement, it’s avoidance. Research cited by the American Psychological Association shows people often steer clear of deeper discussions, especially with those who have opposing views, because they expect there to be some kind of discomfort or conflict. In reality, those conversations are frequently more rewarding and less awkward than anticipated.

“Conversation is this ancient technology for aligning our brains so that we can be on the same page,” said Thalia Wheatley, a Dartmouth College professor quoted by the APA. Yet despite the importance of just having a good talk, many Americans struggle to do effectively, particularly across ideological divides.

That divide is increasingly visible in everyday life, from political debates to family dinners, where conversations can quickly turn into arguments or shut down entirely. Experts say one key shift could help: moving from trying to “win” conversations to trying to understand them.

A meaningful conversation, according to the wellness app Calm’s research, isn’t defined by perfect wording but by presence and the ability to be open, curious and attentive. When people feel heard and understood, even briefly, it can strengthen relationships, reduce stress and build trust.

Studies show those interactions also have measurable mental health benefits. Deeper conversations can lower stress hormones, reduce feelings of loneliness and improve emotional resilience. They also activate parts of the brain associated with connection and reward, helping people feel more grounded and supported.

Still, meaningful dialogue requires effort, and sometimes discomfort.

The APA notes that disagreements are inevitable, but how they are handled determines whether relationships fracture or grow. Researchers have identified techniques that can make tough conversations more productive, including acknowledging the other person’s perspective, finding common ground and reframing statements to reduce defensiveness.

“In any conversation, no matter how much we disagree, we agree on something,” psychologist Julia Minson said in APA research.

That idea aligns with the purpose behind International Day of Mastering Conversations That Matter, which encourages people to engage, not retreat. Find the common ground and love each other on it.

The observance traces its roots to thousands of years of human dialogue. Early debating societies emerged as far back as 5000 B.C., while the Enlightenment era fostered intellectual exchange that shaped modern democratic thought. Today, educators still emphasize communication skills, recognizing that even the best ideas have little impact if they cannot be clearly expressed.

But mastering conversation is not just about speaking. You have to listen too.

Experts point to simple but effective habits like asking open-ended questions, reflecting what others say, paying attention to body language, and resisting the urge to interrupt or dismiss opposing views. Compassion is especially critical, the ability to consider where someone else is coming from, even when you disagree.

That approach may feel small or uncomfortable, but its impact can make all the difference.

In a time when national discourse often feels polarized and impersonal, meaningful conversations offer a way to reconnect, one interaction at a time. Whether it is a discussion with a neighbor, a coworker or a family member, choosing curiosity over confrontation can begin to close gaps that seem otherwise insurmountable.

The message behind the day is pretty clear: differences are not the problem, the inability to talk about them is. So try it. Talk to someone today who doesn’t think like you do, and really just listen. You can defend your thoughts another day. Today just try to learn.

Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced the completion of Operation United Front, a human trafficking operation in Jackson that resulted in two arrests and the recovery of seven victims.

According to Fitch’s office, the operation was carried out April 15 by the attorney general’s Human Trafficking Task Force in coordination with federal, state and local law enforcement agencies.

“My office is committed to taking criminals who traffic people off the streets and equally committed to setting victims on the road to recovery,” Fitch said in a statement. “Developing partnerships with federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies across the State is a priority for the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office, and we are proud to be a part of a network of dedicated law enforcement agencies that work to end human trafficking.”

The attorney general’s office said investigators and prosecutors worked with multiple agencies during the operation, including Alcoholic Beverage Control, the FBI, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, Mississippi Capitol Police, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Jackson Police Department.

Compass Connections, which administers the National Human Trafficking Hotline, observed the operation, including victim advocacy services, according to the attorney general’s office.

The Center for Violence Prevention and Domestic Abuse Family Shelter provided services and treatment to the victims recovered during the operation, officials said.

Fitch’s office said that since launching its “Be the Solution” initiative, it has trained 588 officers across Mississippi. The attorney general’s human trafficking team has also led 62 multi-jurisdictional operations that have resulted in the recovery of 387 victims and 200 arrests, along with additional leads aimed at disrupting trafficking operations across the state.

BILOXI — Reunite Mississippi will host a candlelight vigil this spring on the Mississippi Gulf Coast to honor missing persons and support the families still searching for answers.

The event is scheduled from 6:30 to 8 p.m. at the Biloxi Visitors Center and is intended to bring together families, community members and advocates for an evening of remembrance, unity and awareness.

Organizers say the vigil will provide a space to reflect on the lives of those who remain missing while offering support to loved ones navigating the uncertainty of unresolved cases.

Reunite Mississippi is a nonprofit focused on advancing investigations into missing and unidentified persons across the state through collaboration, innovation and support. The organization works closely with families, law enforcement and forensic professionals to improve case outcomes and ensure families are not left to search alone.

In addition to hosting events like the vigil, the group advocates for families of the missing, promotes information-sharing among agencies and communities, and supports legislation aimed at improving how cases are handled. It also provides training and educational opportunities for law enforcement and medicolegal professionals.

Organizers say their mission is rooted in the belief that every missing person deserves to be found and every family deserves answers.

The upcoming vigil is part of the group’s broader effort to raise awareness and strengthen connections among those affected by missing persons cases throughout Mississippi.

DESOTO COUNTY – DeSoto County Sheriff Thomas Tuggle is urging parents to avoid buying toy guns that closely resemble real firearms, warning that they can create dangerous situations for children and law enforcement.

In a message to the community, Tuggle said realistic-looking toy guns can force deputies to make split-second decisions in situations where it may be impossible to tell whether a weapon is real.

“When a child is holding an object that looks indistinguishable from a real weapon, there’s no time to pause and verify if it’s a toy,” Tuggle said. “Such moments of uncertainty can lead to tragedy, and no parent, officer, or community should bear the burden of a preventable mistake.”

Tuggle said the warning is not about discouraging childhood play, but about making safer choices when it comes to toys that can easily be mistaken for actual firearms.

He encouraged parents to choose brightly colored toy guns that are easier to distinguish from real weapons and to talk with their children about safety, respect for law enforcement and the potential consequences of their actions.

“Our mission is to protect this community every day,” Tuggle said. “Help us keep your children safe through careful decisions that minimize their risk of harm.”

The sheriff’s message came alongside an image showing two handguns and challenging viewers to identify which one was a toy.

JONES COUNTY – A traffic stop late Thursday in Jones County led to the arrest of three men on fentanyl trafficking and other charges, according to the Jones County Sheriff’s Department.

Authorities said Deputy Lou Lowe stopped a passenger vehicle overnight after noticing it had only one working headlight and an expired tag sticker.

The sheriff’s department said there were three men inside the vehicle. After obtaining consent from all three occupants to search the vehicle, Lowe found 196 dosage units of fentanyl, marijuana, drug paraphernalia and two firearms, according to the sheriff’s department.

The three men were arrested and charged as follows:

Raheen Franks, 24, of Quitman, was charged with trafficking fentanyl while in possession of a firearm.

London Bunch, 29, of Waynesboro, was charged with trafficking fentanyl while in possession of a firearm, possession of marijuana in a vehicle and possession of paraphernalia.

Austin Salter, 24, of Buckatunna, was charged with trafficking fentanyl while in possession of a firearm, DUI other and no driver’s license.

Jones County Sheriff’s Department Narcotics Division Sgt. Chase Smith praised the patrol division’s work following the arrests.

“Great job by our Patrol Division, in particular Deputy Lou Lowe, in interdicting these traffickers and getting this deadly drug out of our communities,” Smith said. “We’ve been busy all week making illegal narcotics arrests and putting dealers in jail. Expect that effort to continue unimpeded in the days, weeks, and months ahead.”

WALNUT GROVE – Inmates nearing release at Walnut Grove Correctional Facility are taking part in mock job interviews aimed at helping them prepare to reenter the workforce, according to the Mississippi Department of Corrections.

The department said 13 participants were interviewed this week by staff members, including case managers, alcohol and drug counselors and administrative personnel.

During the interviews, participants discussed employment gaps, personal strengths and common workplace challenges. They were also asked about their skills, interests and how they would respond in job-related situations, MDOC said.

“This is an opportunity for them to prepare for the real thing,” Case Manager Devon Moore said in a statement. “Sitting down and answering questions similar to what an employer would ask helps them build confidence and prepare for employment opportunities.”

MDOC said many of the participants have earned educational and vocational certifications while incarcerated.

Facilitator Vickie Barton said the program is meant to help participants carry those accomplishments with them as they prepare for release.

“This type of preparation reinforces that the work they have done through programs, certifications and classes can be carried forward as they reenter the workforce,” Barton said.

Participants were encouraged to be honest with potential employers about their incarceration and explain how they used their time productively through programs such as anger management, life skills and vocational training.

“Just because someone has a felony conviction does not mean they do not meet the qualifications for employment,” one participant said.

BYHALIA — A Wisconsin man wanted on two counts of child rape was taken into custody Thursday following a vehicle pursuit and manhunt that prompted a temporary school lockdown in the Byhalia area.

Authorities identified the suspect as Robert Gower, who is wanted in Sauk County, Wisconsin, on two counts of child rape.

According to officials, Gower was apprehended by the U.S. Marshals Service, along with deputies from Marshall and DeSoto counties and officers with Byhalia Police.

Investigators said Gower initially fled from law enforcement in a vehicle before abandoning it and running into a wooded area south of East Stonewall Road.

The incident led to a lockdown of nearby schools as a precaution while officers searched for the suspect. The lockdown has since been lifted.

Gower was taken into custody without incident and booked into the DeSoto County Jail as a fugitive from justice. He is also facing additional charges in Mississippi, including disorderly conduct, failure to obey and felony fleeing a law enforcement officer.

He is scheduled to appear in Hernando Circuit Court on the felony fleeing charge. Gower also has a June 26 court date in DeSoto County Circuit Court related to the additional charges.

Authorities said Sauk County is located near the Milwaukee area.

Deputies Ethan Hester and N’shaun Cameron responded to the house and made contact with a male and the missing juvenile, authorities said. After further investigation, the juvenile was safely returned to her mother.

JACKSON — A 67-year-old man has died after being shot inside his home earlier this week, marking the city’s 22nd homicide of the year, according to Jackson police.

Officers with Precinct 3 responded around 2:40 a.m. Tuesday, April 14, to a home in the 2100 block of Summit Street on reports of an aggravated assault and shots fired into an occupied dwelling.

Investigators said Samuel Moore was asleep when gunfire erupted. He told detectives he realized he had been wounded after hearing the shots and said he did not know why anyone would target his home.

Moore was transported to a local hospital with multiple gunshot wounds and was listed in stable condition after speaking with detectives. Authorities said he died Sunday, April 19, from his injuries.

The case is being investigated by the department’s Robbery/Homicide Unit. Police have not identified any suspects and are asking for the public’s help in the investigation.

Anyone with information is urged to contact the Jackson Police Department at 601-960-1234 or Crime Stoppers at 601-355-TIPS.

JACKSON – Jackson State University will receive $500,000 from FedEx over the next four years to support its College of Business, according to JSU.

The university said the funding will help advance student access, faculty excellence and other support initiatives within the college.

According to JSU, the money will support the College of Business’ Supply Chain Management Center and Data Analytics programs in three main areas: student support and empowerment, faculty development and research, and growth initiatives within the Supply Chain Management Center and Data Analytics Lab.

JSU said the latest funding builds on a longstanding relationship between the university and FedEx. Previous collaborations have included the FedEx-JSU Endowed Scholarship Fund and a five-year FedEx-HBCU Student Ambassador program aimed at helping students prepare for the workforce after graduation.

“We are proud to be long-time supporters of the students at Jackson State University,” Rose Jackson Flenorl, manager of Global Citizenship and Human Resources at FedEx, said in the JSU release. “This donation reaffirms our commitment to helping these future leaders access pathways to meaningful careers.”

The Prescription Drug Take Back event is scheduled for Saturday, April 25, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., offering residents a free and anonymous way to discard prescription drugs and vape pens.

JACKSON – Incarcerated youths in state prison were among the competitors and winners last week at Mississippi History Day, part of the National History Day program, demonstrating their ability to compete with traditional students.

This marks the third year students from the Youthful Offender Unit (YOU) have participated in the program. Thirteen students created original history research projects based on the theme “Revolution, Reaction, Reform,” competing in the senior division, individual exhibit category.

At the state competition, YOU School students received three awards, including two special recognitions for projects in Gulf South History and Mississippi History, and a third-place finish in the senior individual exhibit category.

“When students started the program, some believed there was no way they could compete against traditional students,” Education Director Shaniece Mabry said. “After some encouragement, the students lifted their heads and committed to putting forth their best effort.”

Each student developed an exhibit using primary and secondary sources, drawing from materials provided through the Teaching with Primary Sources program, printed online archives, and academic partnerships. Topics ranged from Reconstruction in Mississippi through the life of John R. Lynch to the long-term effects of the Brown v. Board of Education decision in Grenada, Mississippi. Students also researched individuals such as Ruby Doris Smith Robinson and Bettie Mae Fikes.

For many students, this was their first time participating in a competition of this level and presenting formal historical research. Students began the course in October 2025. Research started in February, and project development took place throughout March. The class met weekly, with daily sessions during the final week leading up to competition.

Instructors reported changes in student engagement and behavior throughout the program, including increased participation, improved communication, and stronger accountability.

“Students demonstrated changes in confidence, behavior, and academic engagement,” Instructor Christina Thomas said. “They began thinking before they reacted and expressed a desire to remain in the program.” Students also described the personal impact of participating in the program.

“Competing in National History Day made me do things that I thought I couldn’t,” one student said. “I realized I could achieve anything if I put my mind to it and worked for it. I have heard and learned about history, but I got a deeper understanding when I created history.”

Another student said the class helped improve his presentation and communication skills. The student won a state-level award. “Being able to tell my mother I won Best Project in Gulf South History at the state level is something I will never forget. I’ve never heard my mom sound so proud. For the first time, I can brag on myself in a positive way.”

A third student participating for the first time said, “This program helped keep me out of trouble. I couldn’t participate last year because I kept getting in trouble. I was happy to do something to change my reputation.”

Program leaders emphasized the significance of participation in the competition.

“When students are given the opportunity to engage in this level of academic work, they are participating alongside students from across the state,” Mabry said. “Our students stood shoulder to shoulder with their peers and proved that excellence has no boundaries.”

Support for the program was provided by the Mississippi Humanities Council and funded through the Library of Congress Teaching with Primary Sources Southern Region at Middle Tennessee State University.

Additional support came from staff, volunteers, and partner organizations, including Jackson State University, the Two Mississippi Museums, and the Movement History Initiative.

STARKVILLE — A Starkville Police Department officer critically injured in a February motorcycle crash has reached a major milestone in his recovery, walking out of the hospital after nearly two months of intensive treatment.

Cpl. Colby Huffman, who was hurt Feb. 21 while escorting a funeral detail, is continuing his recovery in Atlanta, where he will undergo four to eight weeks of outpatient therapy, according to an update from his family shared by SPD on April 19.

Huffman had spent 56 days in intensive care and inpatient rehabilitation following the crash, which left him with serious injuries, including head trauma and a broken femur. He was initially airlifted to the University of Mississippi Medical Center before later transferring to a specialized rehabilitation facility in Georgia.

His family said Huffman progressed from critical condition in the ICU to walking on his own after weeks of therapy and multiple medical procedures, including surgery to repair his leg and a tracheostomy to assist with breathing.

“The walk we’ve been waiting for,” his family said in a statement, describing his recovery as a series of “uphill battles” marked by determination and resilience.

Huffman will remain in Atlanta for continued therapy before eventually returning home to Mississippi. His family said they recently relocated to a new apartment during this phase of treatment and encouraged supporters to continue sending messages of encouragement.

The officer’s recovery has drawn widespread community support in Starkville, where residents and local businesses have organized fundraisers to assist with medical and travel expenses.

Huffman was injured in the line of duty while serving the community, and officials have continued to highlight his progress as a sign of hope following the serious crash.

His facial hair is meticulously groomed, and it looks like he spent time, at least on that day, paying close attention to detail.

Four years later, Jessie Young remains missing, with few answers in a case that continues to trouble people who knew him in West Point.

OXFORD — A National Park Service ranger has been recognized by federal prosecutors for his work supporting crime victims following a deadly crash on the Natchez Trace Parkway.

U.S. Attorney Scott Leary announced that Law Enforcement Ranger Dylan Romine received the Carolyn Clayton Victims’ Service Award on April 20 as part of National Crime Victims’ Rights Week in the Northern District of Mississippi.

Romine was honored for his actions following a May 11, 2024, head-on collision on the Natchez Trace Parkway that killed a father and seriously injured a minor child.

Authorities said a 20-year-old driver, under the influence of alcohol, caused the crash. Romine was the first ranger on the scene and worked to ensure the injured child received lifesaving care while also beginning the investigation. His testimony during court proceedings was later described by a U.S. magistrate judge as among the most competent and compelling he had heard from a law enforcement officer.

Officials said the investigation by Romine and other National Park Service rangers ultimately led to a 240-month prison sentence for the defendant.

Beyond his law enforcement duties, Romine was recognized for maintaining contact with the victims’ family, helping them navigate the criminal justice process and ensuring their rights were protected.

“So often we take for granted the wonderful work provided by our law enforcement professionals,” Leary said in a statement. “Dylan Romine embodies the best of what we expect from our men and women who put on a badge.”

Natchez Trace Parkway Superintendent Wendy Hart Ross also praised Romine’s service, saying his work reflects the highest standards of professionalism and care for victims and their families.

The Carolyn Clayton Victims’ Service Award is named for a Mississippi victims’ rights advocate whose efforts helped shape laws supporting crime victims. It is presented by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Mississippi to individuals who demonstrate exceptional service to victims of crime.

PIKE COUNTY – A traffic stop Friday on Interstate 55 led to what authorities believe is one of the largest fentanyl seizures in Pike County history, according to the Pike County Sheriff’s Office.

Sheriff Bryant Wally Jones said the incident happened at about 2:12 p.m. April 17 on northbound I-55 just north of the Summit exit.

According to the sheriff’s office, Jones attempted to stop a dark gray Honda Civic, but the driver continued north before exiting at Dixie Springs. While the vehicle was on the exit ramp, authorities said a large quantity of suspected fentanyl pills was thrown from the passenger window.

The vehicle stopped a short time later, and the driver, identified as Tremail Richardson of Brookhaven, was taken into custody without further incident, the sheriff’s office said. A passenger, identified as Berangton Wells of Wesson, was also taken into custody at the scene.

Richardson was charged with multiple traffic violations and fleeing and eluding law enforcement, according to the sheriff’s office. Authorities said both Richardson and Wells were charged with felony controlled substance violations related to the suspected fentanyl.

The sheriff’s office said the seizure is believed to be one of the largest fentanyl recoveries in Pike County history.

“Fentanyl is claiming lives at an alarming rate,” Jones said in a statement. “We remain committed to proactively and aggressively combating illegal drugs and crime in Pike County. Cases like this highlight the importance of strong law enforcement partnerships.”

Jones also thanked deputies with the Pike County Sheriff’s Office, investigators with the Pike County Gang Unit, the Mississippi Highway Patrol and the Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics for helping apprehend the suspects and assist with the investigation.

The investigation remains ongoing. The sheriff’s office noted that all suspects are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Dr. Shelby Freland Thames, the eighth president of The University of Southern Mississippi and an accomplished research scientist and respected academic leader, passed away Friday, April 17, 2026. His life’s work left a lasting imprint on higher education, scientific research and institutional resilience during one of the most challenging periods in the University’s history.

Thames served as president of Southern Miss from May 1, 2002, to May 20, 2007, following nearly four decades of service to the University as a faculty member and administrator. Over the course of his career, he was recognized nationally as a pioneer in polymer science while also guiding Southern Miss through significant academic growth, capital expansion and disaster recovery.

“Shelby Thames is an iconic force in the history of the University,” said Dr. Joseph S. Paul, president of The University of Southern Mississippi. “His trailblazing work in establishing a polymer science and engineering program that is among the best in the nation was a pioneering catalyst, propelling the journey to our current status as a Carnegie R1 Research Institution.”

A native son of Southern Miss, Thames earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in chemistry from the University before completing a doctorate in organic chemistry at the University of Tennessee. He joined the Southern Miss faculty in 1964 and went on to establish what would become one of the nation’s most respected polymer science programs. Under his leadership, the program earned national distinction for being among the first in the country to offer bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in polymer science, ultimately evolving into today’s School of Polymer Science and Engineering.

“As a result of Dr. Thames’ leadership for academic excellence, The University of Southern Mississippi enjoys global recognition in the field of polymer science and engineering through significant research funding and contributions aligned with evolving areas of critical need and by consistent recognition of our graduates validated through their employment and growth within the world’s most prominent institutions of science and engineering,” said Dr. Jeffrey Wiggins, distinguished professor of polymer science and engineering at Southern Miss. “Professor Thames displayed remarkable vision when he established polymer science and engineering at Southern Miss in the 1970s, at a time when the field was essentially nonexistent as formal undergraduate and graduate degree programs. His dream has given us purpose and profoundly changed our lives, and he will be dearly missed by our community.”

Thames founded the Thames‑Rawlins Research Group and built a research legacy centered on advanced polymers, coatings and high‑performance materials. His work helped secure the University’s first federally funded research facility and positioned Southern Miss as a leader in polymer research and engineering for generations of scholars and students.

“Professor Thames laid the foundation for polymer science and engineering at Southern Miss, and that foundation continues to shape who we are today,” said Dr. Derek Patton, professor and director of the Southern Miss School of Polymer Science and Engineering. “His vision established not only an academic program, but a culture of rigor, innovation and impact that remains central to our mission. As we reflect on his passing, we are reminded that our responsibility is not only to honor what he built, but to advance it through the success of our students, the strength of our research and the broader contributions of our community. I see his influence daily, in the expectations we set, the students we train and the impact our faculty pursue. His vision created an enduring legacy, and with that comes a responsibility to sustain it with the same level of ambition and purpose. He will be deeply missed.”

As University president, Thames led a period of sustained progress that included expansion of doctoral programs, record fundraising and major capital improvements. Projects completed during his administration included the Thad Cochran Student Center, the Trent Lott National Center for Excellence in Economic Development and Entrepreneurship, the International Center, additions to the Polymer Science Research Center and the initial development of the Innovation and Commercialization Park.

Perhaps most notably, Thames’ presidency was defined by his leadership following Hurricane Katrina in 2005. The catastrophic storm caused nearly $290 million in damage to University facilities and severely disrupted operations across all campuses and teaching sites. Despite the devastation, Thames was resolute in his commitment to protect Southern Miss employees and restore the institution’s mission.

With determined optimism and steady leadership, Thames reassured a shaken University community that Southern Miss would emerge stronger. Classes resumed on the Hattiesburg campus within two weeks of the storm and on the Gulf Coast within six weeks, a testament to his resolve, preparation and belief in the institution and its people.

“Dr. Thames ushered in economic development as part of our mission,” added Paul. “And his work as president in re-opening after Hurricane Katrina with no loss of jobs, was truly heroic.”

Following the conclusion of his presidential service in 2007, Thames returned to the faculty, continuing his work as an esteemed polymer scientist until retiring in 2012 as a Distinguished University Research Professor Emeritus.

“Decades before sustainability became central to polymer science, Shelby Thames was already there, transforming Mississippi tung oil and other agricultural building blocks into high‑performance coatings and championing waterborne, low‑VOC chemistries that now define much of our field and industry,” Patton added. “The School of Polymer Science and Engineering stands on the intellectual framework he established, captured in his oft‑repeated phrase, ‘It’s all in the chemistry,’ and on his insistence that discoveries of global consequence could emerge from Hattiesburg, Mississippi. Those of us now charged with advancing this mission do so with profound gratitude for the courage, curiosity and conviction he brought to every problem he pursued.”

In addition to his leadership roles as a scholar and administrator, Thames was a steadfast supporter of the University throughout his life. He was honored for his contributions with induction into the Athletic Department’s M‑Club Hall of Fame in 2007 and The University of Southern Mississippi Alumni Hall of Fame in 2002. Thames and his wife, Shirley, are members of the Athletic Department’s Circle of Champions, the USM Foundation’s Honor Club at the Black and Gold Society level and life members of the Alumni Association.

The Shelby F. Thames and Shirley D. Thames Scholarship for High Ability Students Endowment was created in 2002, with a vision for recruiting students with tremendous academic achievement through scholarship support. Gifts to this scholarship in memory of Dr. Shelby F. Thames may be made online at USMFoundation.com/Thames.

Visitation will be held Friday, April 24 from 5-8 p.m. in Bennett Auditorium on the campus of The University of Southern Mississippi. The service will be held on Saturday, April 25 at 10 a.m. in Bennett Auditorium, followed by burial in Highland Cemetery.

His life’s work left a lasting imprint on higher education, scientific research and institutional resilience during one of the most challenging periods in the University’s history.

JACKSON – Three people have been arrested as part of an investigation into unemployment compensation fraud known as Operation Payback, according to State Auditor Shad White.

White said special agents with the State Auditor’s Office arrested Chadwick Stubbs, Blair Stubbs and Shinka Stubbs.

According to the auditor’s office, the three are accused of submitting fraudulent unemployment claims using the identities of 13 inmates who were incarcerated with Blair and Chadwick Stubbs when the claims were filed with the Mississippi Department of Employment Security.

“My office discovered that during COVID, Mississippi handed out over half a billion dollars in improper unemployment payments,” White said in a statement. “We will continue working diligently to hold criminals accountable and recover as much of this misspent money as possible.”

If convicted, the three could face up to $36,000 in fines and up to 45 years in prison, according to the auditor’s office.

The State Auditor’s Office said all people arrested are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in court.

The office also said suspected fraud can be reported through the auditor’s website or by calling 1-800-321-1275 during normal business hours.

HATTIESBURG – The Hattiesburg Zoo has introduced three baby spider monkeys making their public debut this week.

The zoo said the monkeys, named Cider, Holly and Juniper, arrived in late 2025 and have spent the past several months growing and receiving around-the-clock care in the zoo’s quarantine facility.

According to the zoo, each monkey was smaller than a sweet potato when they arrived and needed bottle feedings five times a day. They have since grown to about the size of a pineapple and still receive two bottle feedings daily as they continue to develop.

Zoo officials said animal care and veterinary staff have focused on bottle feedings, gradual introductions to solid foods, regular weight checks, health assessments, enrichment activities, socialization and routine wellness exams.

Guests can now see the three monkeys inside the Asbury Discovery Center in a special indoor glass viewing area, according to the zoo. The space is intended to help the animals safely adjust to new sights, sounds and people after spending their early months primarily with their care team.

The zoo said it will still be some time before the monkeys are ready to join the rest of the spider monkey troop on the South America Boardwalk. Officials said the gradual introduction is designed to ensure the young monkeys are strong, confident and socially prepared.

JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Corrections is highlighting services available to crime victims through its Division of Victim Services, which provides notifications, resources and support to those impacted by crime.

The division’s primary role is to notify registered victims prior to an inmate’s release, as well as in cases of escape, recapture or death while in custody. Officials say the program is designed to ensure victims remain informed and involved throughout the criminal justice process.

The Division of Victim Services also offers referrals for counseling, crisis intervention, support groups and information about compensation programs. Staff assist victims with questions about inmate status, parole conditions and other public information.

According to the agency, victims must register with the division to receive notifications. Once enrolled, they are entitled to updates, including notice within 15 days before an inmate’s release or following significant changes in custody status.

The program operates a toll-free hotline available 24/7, allowing victims to request information, update contact details and learn how to submit statements for parole or pardon consideration.

Officials say the division also works to train corrections staff on victim sensitivity and collaborates with service providers across the state to improve resources and communication.

The services are part of broader protections outlined in the Mississippi Crime Victims’ Bill of Rights, which guarantees victims access to information and participation in the justice process.

The Division of Victim Services can be reached at 601-359-5628 during business hours or toll-free at 1-866-522-4087.
